bull.argument: Amazon's filing shows a business compounding at scale. Consolidated net sales rose 12% to $716.9 billion in 2025, and AWS grew 20% to $128.7 billion, with operating income for AWS reaching $45.6 billion. Total operating income climbed to $80.0 billion from $68.6 billion. Operating cash flow reached $139.5 billion, up from $115.9 billion. The company's stated financial focus is long-term, sustainable growth in free cash flow, and it is investing heavily to build that future: cash capital expenditures rose to $128.3 billion, mostly to support AWS growth. Management also guided Q1 2026 net sales growth of 11% to 15%. The filing is candid that free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion because of this spending, and that AI investments carry write-down risk. Still, the operating engine is strengthening, the balance sheet holds $123.0 billion in cash and marketable securities, and no borrowings were outstanding under the revolving credit facilities or commercial paper programs.

claims.claim: AWS sales grew 20% in 2025, a strong growth rate for the segment.
claims.quote: AWS sales increased 20% in 2025, compared to the prior year.

claims.claim: Operating cash flow rose substantially in 2025.
The company had no borrowings outstanding under its revolving credit facilities or commercial paper programs at year-end 2025.
claims.quote: We had no borrowings outstanding under the two unsecured revolving credit facilities or the commercial paper programs as of December 31, 2025.

bear.argument: The bull case rests on operating growth, but the filing shows that growth is being bought with cash. Free cash flow fell from $38.2 billion to $11.2 billion, a drop of roughly 71%, because cash capital expenditures rose to $128.3 billion. Operating cash flow of $139.5 billion was almost entirely consumed by that spending. Investing outflows reached $142.5 billion, and the company turned to external funding, with long-term debt rising from $52.6 billion to $65.6 billion and financing inflows of $25.0 billion in 2025. The filing also warns that AI and new-technology investments may be written down or written off if benefits fail to materialize, and that technology infrastructure spending will increase further. Operating income also absorbed a $2.5 billion FTC settlement and $2.7 billion of severance charges. Investors are being asked to trust that enormous, rising spending will pay off, while the filing itself says those returns are uncertain.

The company now relies on new borrowing to fund investment

claims.claim: AI and new investments may be written down and fail to pay back
claims.quote: Failure to realize the benefits of amounts we invest in new technologies, products, or services could result in the value of those investments being written down or written off.

bull.argument: The bear case is right about the cash math but wrong about what it means. Free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion because capital spending rose to $128.3 billion, and the filing says that spending is mostly for AWS infrastructure, with AWS sales up 20% and AWS operating income up to $45.6 billion. Spending that is already producing growth and profit at the segment level is different from speculative spending. Operating cash flow still rose to $139.5 billion, and the company funded the gap while holding $123.0 billion in cash and marketable securities. The debt rise to $65.6 billion is real, and the filing does not hide it, but the company also says it had no borrowings outstanding under its revolving credit facilities or commercial paper programs at year-end 2025. The $2.5 billion FTC charge and $2.7 billion severance are one-time items that the filing itemizes, and they are not evidence of a weakening core. The filing does warn of write-off risk, and I concede that. Investors must judge whether returns arrive, but the reported results so far are growing, not shrinking.

claims.claim: AWS operating income rose, showing the infrastructure spending is producing profit in that segment.
Management ties the bulk of capital spending to AWS growth, not to unproven ventures.
claims.quote: which primarily reflect investments in technology infrastructure (the majority of which is to support AWS business growth)

claims.claim: The company had substantial liquidity at year-end 2025.
claims.quote: our cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities balances, which, at fair value, were $101.2 billion and $123.0 billion as of December 31, 2024 and 2025.

bear.argument: The bull case concedes the cash math but argues the spending is already paying off. The filing does not support that comfort. AWS operating income rose, but the filing attributes the AWS margin pressure to 'spending on technology infrastructure' and says technology infrastructure spending will increase over time, so the segment's profit is absorbing rising costs that are not yet cash-generative at the company level. Free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion, and management's own framing is that free cash flow was $38.2 billion the prior year, a 71% decline. Being cash-funded by $123.0 billion in liquidity does not remove the fact that financing inflows of $25.0 billion were needed in 2025 and long-term debt rose to $65.6 billion; the 'no revolver borrowings' point describes one facility, not the total debt load. Calling the $2.5 billion FTC settlement and $2.7 billion severance 'one-time' understates the pattern: the filing also lists lease liabilities rising to $87.3 billion and warns that new-technology investments may be written off. Growth is real, but the cash returns on this spending are unproven.

judge.reasoning: The bull's Round 2 AWS operating income quote failed verification, which weakens its central claim that spending is already producing segment profit, while its other quotes were verified. The bear's evidence is consistently verified and it directly engaged the bull's AWS-profit argument, noting that rising infrastructure costs absorb that profit and that the revolver point covers only one facility. The bear therefore edges out the bull on evidence and responsiveness.
